text: Kim Thompson (September 25, 1956 – June 19, 2013) was an American comic book editor, translator, and publisher, best known as vice president and co-publisher of Seattle-based Fantagraphics Books. Along with co-publisher Gary Groth, Thompson worked to promote alternative comics in the American market and made it his mission to introduce European cartoonists' work to American readers. Born in Denmark in 1956, Thompson was the child of a government contractor father and had a Danish mother, growing up speaking Danish, a skill that supported his later work as a translator; he was also fluent in French. He developed an early passion for comics, particularly the works of André Franquin, Maurice Tillieux, Jacques Tardi, and Jean "Mœbius" Giraud, and contributed letters to American superhero comic book columns such as Amazing Spider-Man, Captain America, Conan the Barbarian, Incredible Hulk, Iron Man, Marvel Spotlight, and Marvel-Two-in-One. His early writing appeared in the fanzine Omniverse in 1979. Thompson moved to the United States in 1977, met Groth through a mutual friend, joined Fantagraphics' staff that year, and soon became a co-owner. In 1978, he saved the company from bankruptcy by using his inheritance. He was a regular contributor to The Comics Journal since 1977, where he reviewed Dave Sim's Cerebus and later criticized Sim for controversial statements on feminism and self-publishing. He also wrote for the defunct magazine Amazing Heroes from 1981 to 1987. Since Fantagraphics began publishing comics in 1982, Thompson edited many of its popular titles, including Peter Bagge's Hate, Chris Ware's Acme Novelty Library, Joe Sacco's Palestine, Stan Sakai's Usagi Yojimbo, Linda Medley's Castle Waiting, and anthologies like Critters and Zero Zero. His last major release was a remastered and expanded edition of Guy Peellaert's The Adventures of Jodelle (1966), which he also translated from French. As a long-time champion of European comics, Thompson translated works by numerous international cartoonists published by Fantagraphics and used in The Comics Journal, including Nikoline Werdelin (Danish), Joost Swarte (Dutch), David B., Emile Bravo, Killoffer, Jacques Tardi, and Lewis Trondheim (French), Nicolas Mahler (German), Gabriella Giandelli, Igort, Leila Marzocchi, and Sergio Ponchione (Italian), Jason (Norwegian or French), Max (Spanish), and Martin Kellerman (Swedish). He noted that while he did not speak all these languages, he could read them, with Danish being his native language and Swedish and Norwegian being close to it; he learned Spanish in high school and studied German in high school, and his Italian was weak, relying on French, Spanish, and dictionaries, always checked with authors. On March 6, 2013, Thompson announced he had lung cancer and took a leave of absence to undergo treatment; he died on June 19, 2013, at age 56, survived by his wife Lynn Emmert, mother, father, and brother. He received an Inkpot Award in 2001 and was a 1996 Will Eisner Comic Industry Awards nominee for Best Editor for The Acme Novelty Library, Palestine, and Zero Zero. In October 2021, he was posthumously awarded the inaugural Tom Spurgeon Award at the Cartoon Crossroads Columbus’ seventh festival, alongside Mollie Slott and Orrin C. Evans, recognizing non-cartoonists' contributions to the comics medium. Comics journalist Tom Spurgeon described Thompson as a key figure in transforming Fantagraphics into a significant publisher and praised his advocacy for French-language comics, noting his translations were idiomatic and natural in English. Comics critic R. Fiore highlighted that Thompson's work brought French comics to English readers in a way that surpassed even the best translations by Anthea Bell and Derek Hockridge, calling his contributions a significant creative loss.
